The Marbled octopus Amphioctopus aegina exhibits a life-history strategy finely tuned to warm tropical waters. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 29.7 °C [T = 29.7 °C], newly hatched paralarvae emerge from their egg capsules after an embryonic period of 18.3 days [ab = 18.3 days], a developmental duration that aligns closely with estimates for congeneric species at similar thermal regimes. At the moment of hatching, these planktonic individuals possess a mean wet weight of only 0.00019 grams [Wwb = 0.00019 grams], a remarkably diminutive starting mass that underscores the extreme fecundity required to offset the high mortality typical of the pelagic larval stage. This neonatal mass represents one of the smallest recorded among coastal octopus species, reflecting the trade-off between offspring size and the total number of propagules produced per brood.

As the paralarvae transition into benthic juveniles and begin their rapid somatic growth phase, the divergence in body mass trajectories between males and females becomes increasingly apparent. Puberty, defined as the attainment of functional reproductive maturity, is reached when individuals achieve a wet body weight of approximately 21.0 grams [Wwp = approximately 21.0 grams]. This threshold is derived from the point at which the time-weight growth curves of the sexes begin to diverge significantly, marking the onset of differential energy investment into gamete production versus continued somatic expansion. Under the consistent thermal conditions of 29.7 °C [T = 29.7 °C], this critical developmental milestone is attained relatively early in the life cycle, allowing individuals to transition to the reproductive phase while still undergoing considerable somatic growth. This pubertal mass is modest compared to the maximum sizes reported for the species, indicating a strategy of early maturation.

The ongoing growth trajectory culminates in a peak recorded wet weight of 156.0 grams [Wwi = 156.0 grams] measured at an age of 160 days. This value, however, is somewhat lower than the maximum estimate of 400 grams reported in some fisheries databases, a discrepancy that may reflect differences in local prey availability, habitat quality, or population-specific genetic variation in growth capacity. Under the stable temperature regime of 29.7 °C [T = 29.7 °C], this mass is achieved concurrently with the species' maximum recorded lifespan, suggesting that growth decelerates markedly once individuals approach their ultimate size. The substantial increase from the pubertal mass of 21.0 grams to this adult peak highlights the considerable energetic investment in somatic tissue that occurs during the sub-adult phase.

Female Marbled octopus exhibit a highly fecund, semelparous reproductive strategy, with total lifetime fecundity culminating in the deposition of a single, large brood shortly before senescence and death. At 29.7 °C [T = 29.7 °C], a female will deposit an average of 6900.0 eggs  over the course of her sole reproductive event, a cumulative reproductive output that likely approaches her maximum physiological capacity. This immense clutch size is a direct consequence of the minuscule hatchling mass of 0.00019 grams, as the energetic cost per egg is minimized, allowing the female to allocate a large proportion of her total body reserves to egg production. The timing of this single spawning event is tightly linked to the species lifespan, with brooding and subsequent death occurring shortly after egg deposition. Such extreme fecundity is a common adaptation among cephalopods with small paralarvae, enabling the species to overcome the substantial losses experienced during the vulnerable planktonic phase in tropical waters where predation pressure is typically high.

The entire life cycle of Amphioctopus aegina, from hatching to completion of the reproductive phase, is remarkably compressed. At 29.7 °C [T = 29.7 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan from hatching to natural death is 160.0 days [am = 160.0 days], a duration typical of many small, warm-water octopus species that exhibit a 'live fast, die young' life-history strategy. The post-hatching lifespan available for growth and reproduction amounts to approximately 142 days, within which the animal must grow from a planktonic larva weighing 0.00019 grams [Wwb = 0.00019 grams] to a reproductively mature adult exceeding 21.0 grams [Wwp = 21.0 grams]. The remarkable efficiency of this rapid life cycle is predicated on the warm, stable thermal environment, which elevates metabolic and growth rates to allow the species to exploit ephemeral resources and high predation pressures characteristic of tropical coastal ecosystems.
